name: Henry V of England
summary: Henry V ruled as a hereditary Lancastrian king who revived the English claim to the French crown, conquered Normandy and secured succession to France at Troyes in 1420. At home he enforced religious orthodoxy, crushed the Lollard rising of Sir John Oldcastle and the Southampton plot, and guarded royal rights against the papacy. Most of his recorded positions concern kingship, war and the Church; he left little on economic or social questions.

notes:
Shakespeare's play was not used. No answers rest on the 1419 ordinances of war or Henry's will (see notFound). Chambers and Daunt's A Book of London English could not be opened; the letters were read through British History Online summaries and Riley's Memorials. Agincourt prisoner killing and the Rouen expulsion are recorded in sources but match no statement.

Merged with an independent claude-haiku-5-5 audit: 3 answers taken from it, 11 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-haiku-5-5 notes: Two chroniclers' reports (the Gesta Henrici Quinti and the reported reply to the Dauphin's tennis-balls taunt) were not used for any answer because they are secondhand and not opened in full; this audit rests on the London record of his 1415 speech and on secondary summaries of his acts. Most answers are record-based rather than statements of principle, so they are medium at most. Inclusion is expected to fail: the record here is thin on his own stated views.

Second Sonnet pass (2026-11-20): added Britannica, Tyler's Memoirs (Gutenberg 20489) and the Treaty of Troyes extracts as sources; replaced Wikipedia-only support; themes searched: war and territory, heresy and religion, treason and punishment, hereditary rule, language policy. Economy, society, liberty, ecology and technology had nothing that settles any statement.
